why: NI into retained earnings, the roll-forward
answer: Net income goes into retained earnings in shareholders' equity. So ending retained earnings is the beginning balance plus net income minus any dividends paid.

why: says net income goes into cash on the balance sheet directly
answer: Net income goes straight into the cash account on the balance sheet, because profit is cash the company earned, so cash goes up by net income.

why: non-cash expense, lowers pre-tax income and taxes, NI down; added back on CFS
answer: A goodwill impairment is a non-cash expense on the income statement, so it lowers pre-tax income, which also lowers taxes a bit, and net income goes down. On the cash flow statement you add it back since no cash left the business, and goodwill on the balance sheet goes down by the impairment.

why: says impairment doesn't touch net income, only the balance sheet
answer: Goodwill impairment doesn't affect net income at all, it just reduces goodwill on the balance sheet and equity, because it's non-cash.

why: accelerated, bigger early tax shields, earlier cash worth more
answer: Accelerated depreciation gives the higher DCF value. It front-loads the tax deductions, so you save more on taxes in the early years and free cash flow is higher sooner, and earlier cash flows are worth more because they're discounted less. Total depreciation is the same either way, it's just the timing.
Straight-line gives a higher valuation, because it keeps depreciation lower in the early years, so profits look higher and the company is worth more.

Enterprise value doesn't change. The company borrows $100 and pays it all out as a dividend, so debt goes up by $100 and equity value goes down by $100 because that cash left to shareholders. Those offset, so EV stays the same.

why: says EV goes up by the new debt
answer: Enterprise value goes up by $100, because the company took on $100 of new debt and EV includes debt.

why: price/sales is the invalid one, EV pairs with pre-interest metrics, price with NI
answer: EV to sales, EV to EBITDA and P/E are fine, but price to sales doesn't make sense conceptually. Enterprise value should go with metrics that are available to all investors before interest, like sales and EBITDA, and equity value goes with net income, which is after interest. Price to sales mixes equity value with sales, which belongs to everyone.

why: WACC up, value down; buyer can pay less, LBO returns lower
answer: If the cost of debt goes up, the WACC goes up, so the present value of the cash flows is lower and the valuation drops. For a buyer, financing is more expensive, so they can't pay as much and still hit their returns. In an LBO, more cash goes to interest, so there's less to pay down debt and the IRR is lower.

why: says WACC falls and the value rises
answer: When the cost of debt goes up, the WACC actually goes down because debt has a tax shield, so the valuation goes up. Buyers would be happier.

why: saves cash early, balance compounds, higher exit debt lowers returns
answer: PIK debt helps early cash flow because the interest isn't paid in cash, it gets added to the balance. That frees up cash to pay down the senior debt. But the PIK balance compounds, so you have more debt at exit, which eats into the equity value and lowers returns unless the company grows enough.
